content: Additionally, the group challenges medical claims regarding the health risks associated with smoking. FOREST describes itself as the voice and friend of the smoker and receives most of its funding from the tobacco industry. The organization was officially established in 1979 by Sir Christopher Foxley-Norris, a former Air Chief Marshal. In 1987, Lord Harris of High Cross, who served as the general director of the Institute of Economic Affairs from 1957 to 1989, was appointed as chairman. He held this position until his death in October 2006 at the age of 81. Lord Harris, a long-time pipe smoker and vocal critic of public smoking bans, authored numerous articles and essays on the topic of passive smoking, also referred to as second-hand smoke, sidestream smoke, or environmental tobacco smoke. One of his notable works, Smoking Out The Truth: a challenge to the Chief Medical Officer (2005), questioned the prevailing medical consensus on the dangers of passive smoking. FOREST representatives frequently appear on British television and radio programs and are often quoted in newspapers across the United Kingdom. The organization’s website openly states that it is funded mainly by the tobacco industry. However, critics have alleged that FOREST is an astroturf group, meaning it was created to appear as a grassroots movement while actually being orchestrated by the tobacco industry. Specifically, it has been suggested that FOREST’s establishment was planned by the Tobacco Advisory Committee (TAC), the trade association representing the British tobacco industry. Minutes from a 1979 meeting of the TAC’s Public Relations Sub-Committee reportedly document discussions about the creation of FOREST. In recent years, FOREST has garnered support from several prominent individuals who are smokers, including artist David Hockney, inventor Trevor Baylis, musician Joe Jackson, restaurateur and television chef Antony Worrall Thompson, and Claire Fox, the director of the Institute of Ideas. In September 2005, Hockney, Jackson, and Fox spoke at a fringe meeting organized by FOREST during the Labour Party conference in Brighton. Despite its efforts, FOREST was unable to prevent the implementation of a total ban on smoking in enclosed public spaces in England, which came into effect in the summer of 2007. This ban applies to all pubs, bars, cafés, restaurants, workplaces, and private members' clubs. Similar bans were introduced in Northern Ireland in spring 2007, Wales in April 2007, and Scotland in March 2006. Nevertheless, FOREST has vowed to continue advocating for what it calls freedom of choice. The group’s current slogans include Smokers are voters, too, Enough is enough, and Nanny state? No thanks.
